  alia his sim̅ ubi aspiratione . ut dicitur gah libeda _jah libaida_
      diptongon _ai_ pro e longa    p ch _q_ ponunt.--Cp. § 1, n. 5,
  and, for explanation, especially Kirchhoff, p. 20 et seq.




CHAP. II. THE VOWELS.


a

§ 3. The Gothic =a= signifies as a rule the short a-sound [as in G.
mann].

  NOTE 1. Foren words and names; as, =Annas=, Ἀννας; =Akaja=, Ἀχαΐα;
  =barbarus=, βάρβαρος; =aggilus=, ἄγγελος; =karkara=, _carcer_;
  =lukarn=, _lucerna_; =Kafarnaum=, Καπερναούμ.

  NOTE 2. Gothic names: =Athanaricus=, =Ariaricus=, =Amalafrigda=
  (_Ammian._)

§ 4. Short =a= is very frequent both in stem-syllabls and in
inflection. E. g.

(a) Stem-syllabls: =agis=, _aw_; =aljis=, '_alius_'; =tagr=, _tear_;
=aƕa=, '_aqua_'; =alan=, _to grow_; =hafjan=, _to heav_; =saltan=, _to
salt_; =haldan=, _to hold_; =waldan=, _to rule_; =fadar=, _father_;
=staþs=, _place_.--=ahtau=, '_octo_'; =gasts=, _guest_; =ƕaþar=,
'_uter_'; =awistr=, _sheepfold_ (OHG. au, '_ovis_'; ahd. gr., § 219, n.
3); =bandi=, _band_; =barn=, _child_; =saggws=, _song_; all preterits
of the III.-V. ablaut-series: =bar=, _I bore_; =hlaf=, _I stole_;
=band=, _I bound_; =gaf=, _I gave_, etc.

(b) Inflections: =daga= (dat. sg., § 90), =waúrda= (nom. acc. pl., §
93), =giba= (nom. acc. sg., § 96), =guma= (nom. sg., § 107), =haírtôna=
(nom. acc. pl., § 109); --=blindamma=, =blindana=, =blinda=, =blindata=
(str. adj., § 123); --=imma=, =ina=, =ita=, =ija=, =meina= (prn.; § 150
et seq.); --=nima= (1st pers. sg. prs. ind.); =nimaima=, =nimaiwa=,
=nimaina= (1st pers. pl. du. and 3d pers. pl. opt., § 170); =haitada=
(medio-passiv, § 170); =sôkida= (weak prt., § 184); --adverbs: =-ba=
(as, =glaggwuba=), =nêƕa=, =inna=, =ana=, =waíla=, etc.

  NOTE 1. Apocope of an unaccented =a= before enclitics:
  =þat-ist=, =þat-ei=, =þan-uh=, =þamm-uh=, =þan-ei=, =þamm-ei=,
  =kar-ist=.--Also =frêt= and =frêtum= (prt. of =fra-itan=, _to
  devour_, § 176, n. 3).

  NOTE 2. For =a= in the difthongs =ai=, =au=, s. §§ 21. 25.

§ 5. In a few cases =a= is long [as in E. father]. (Comp. Holtzmann,
Altd. Gr., I, 3 et seq.).

(a) In foren words: =Silbânus= (_Silvanus_), =aurâli= (_orale_),
=spaíkulâtur= (_speculator_), =Peilâtus=, etc.;

(b) In the following Gothic words: =fâhan= (OHG. fâhan), _to cach_;
=hâhan= (OHG. hâhan), _to hang_; =þâhta= (prt. of =þagkjan=, _to
think_); =brâhta= (prt. of =briggan=, _to bring_); =gafâhs=, _a haul_;
=faúrhâh=, _curtain_; =gahâhjô=, _in order_; =-gâhts=, _a going_; also
=þâhô= (OHG. dâha), _clay_; =unwâhs=, _blameless_ (OE. wôh, _wrong_).

  NOTE. In the words mentiond under (b) =âh= arose from =anh= (§ 50,
  n. 1). Cp. also Litbl. 1886, p. 485.


e

§ 6. =e= is always a long, close vowel (=ê=) approaching very much the
sound of =i= [as in E. they].

  NOTE 1. In Greek words η is regularly represented by =ê=; e.
  g., =Gabriêl=, =Kêfas=, =aíkklêsjô=, =Krêta=; --sumtimes also
  ι: =Naên=, Ναίν; =Tykêkus=, Τυχικός; =aíloê=, ἐλωί; likewise e:
  =Jarêd=, Ἰαρέδ.

  NOTE 2. In Gothic names Latin writers employ =e= for Gothic =ê=:
  =Sigismêres=, =Gelimêr=, =Reccarêd=; besides, as erly as the 6th
  century, quite regularly also =i=; as, =Theodemir=, =Valamir=. Cp.
  Beitr., 11, 7 et seq.; Wrede, Wand., 92 et seq. #/Ναίν

§ 7. Goth. =ê= (which regularly corresponds to OHG. and OS. â; ahd.
gr., § 34) is found:

(a) in reduplicating verbs, in part with the ablaut =ô= (§§ 179.
181): =grêtan=, =lêtan=, =slêpan=; (b) in the prt. pl. of the IV.
and V. ablaut-series: =sêtum= (inf. =sitan=, _to sit_), =nêmun= (inf.
=niman=, _to take_), =têmum= (inf. =timan=, _to befit_), =êtum= (inf.
_itan_), and in the prt. sg. =frêt=; Luc. XV, 30 (§ 176, n. 3); (c)
in derivativs from the verbal stems givn under (b); as, =andanêms=,
_agreeabl_; =andanêm=, _a receiving_; =gatêmiba=, _becumingly_;
=uzêta=, _manger_; (d) in other words; as, =jêr=, _year_; =qêns=,
_wife_; =mêna=, _moon_; =lêkeis=, _fysician_; =mêrjan=, _to preach_;
=manasêþs= ('_man-seed_'), _world_, etc.; (e) in formativ syllabls:
=fahêþs=, _joy_; =awêþi=, _flock of sheep_ (cp. however § 17, n. 1);
=azêts=, _easy_; 2nd pers. sg. prt. of wvs., =-dês= (=nasidês=, § 184);
(f) final: in the ending of the gen. pl.; as, =dagê=; in monosyllabic
instrumentals: =þê=, =ƕê= (§§ 153. 159); in particls and advs.; as,
=swê=, =untê=, =hidrê=, =bisunjanê=; lastly, in the dativs =ƕammêh=,
=ƕarjammêh=, =ainummê-hun= (cp. §§ 163-166).

  NOTE 1. =ê= before vowels appears as =ai=; s. § 22.

  NOTE 2. =ei= occurs quite often for =ê=, especially in the Gospel
  of St. Luke; as, =qeins= (= =qêns=), =faheid= (= =fahêd=),
  =fraleitais= (= =fralêtais=); Lu. II, 5. 10. 29; =afleitan=; Mt.
  IX, 6, etc.

  NOTE 3. Sporadically also =i= for =ê=; so, frequently, in the
  Gospel of St. Lu.; as, =b~i~rusjôs=; Lu. II, 41; =q~i~þeina=; VIII,
  56. IX, 21; =tawid~i~deina=; VI, 11; =duatsn~i~wun=; Mk. VI, 53.
  Only =i= is found in =wriþus=, _herd_; Lu. VIII, 33 (for =wrêþus=;
  cp. Bezzenb. Beitr. 3, 114).

  NOTE 4. Reversely, also =e= occurs for =i= and =ei= (§ 10, n. 5; §
  17, n. 1).--These deviations (in ns. 2-4) seem due to East Gothic
  writers; cp. Wrede, 'Ostg.', 161.

§ 8. From the preceding =ê= must be separated the =ê= of sum Gothic
words in which it corresponds to OHG. ea, ia (not â): =hêr=, _here_;
=Krêks=, _Greek_; =fêra=, _side_, _region_; =mês=, _table_. Cp. ahd.
gr., §§ 35. 36; Beitr., 18, 409 et seq.


i

§ 9. Gothic =i=, as a rule, denotes the short vowel =i= [as in E. it],
while its corresponding long sound is represented by =ei= [= ie in E.
believ]; s. § 16.

  NOTE 1. The =i= in Greek words stands for short ι, only
  exceptionally for η which is generally represented by =ê=; e. g.,
  =Aúnisimus=, Ὀνήσιμος; =Biþania=, Βηθανία.

  NOTE 2. =i= in Gothic words is long, when it is incorrectly employd
  for =ê= (cp. § 7, n. 3).

§ 10. The Gothic =i=, from an historical point of view, is of two
kinds: It represents two originally distinct sounds which, from a
purely Gothic standpoint, can not be separated.

(a) Goth. =i= = proethnic Germanic e (OHG. ë or i; cp. ahd. gr., §§
28-30), as in the prs. tense of verbs of the III.-V. ablaut-series
(§§ 32-34): =niman=, OHG. nëman; =giban=, OHG. gëban; =giba=, OHG.
gëba; =bindan=, OHG. bintan; =itan=, _to eat_; =midjis=, '_medius_';
=hlifan=, _to steal_; =swistar=, OHG. swëster; =fidwôr=, _four_;
=gifts=, _gift_; =-qiss=, _speech_; the pps. of the V. ablaut-series:
=gibans=, =itans=, =lisans=, =wigans=, =qiþans=.

(b) Goth. =i= = proethnic Germanic i (OHG. i; ahd. gr., § 31); e. g.,
=lists=, _stratagem_; =fisks=, _fish_; =is=, _he_; =wissa=, _I knew_;
=skritnan=, _to rend_ (intr.); prt. pl. and pp. of the verbs of the
I. ablaut-series (§ 30): =bitun=, =bitans= (inf. =beitan=); =stigun=,
=stigans= (inf. =steigan=); =liþun=, =liþans= (inf. =leiþan=).

  NOTE 1. Final =i= occurs in =ni=, =bi=, =si=, =hiri=; in the
  nominativs of feminin and neuter =j=-stems: =bandi= (§ 96), =kuni=
  (§ 93); in the acc. and voc. sg. of the masculin =j=-stems: =hari=
  (§ 90); 3d pers. sg. prt. opt.: =nêmi=. This final =i= appears as
  =j=, when it becums medial (§ 45).

  NOTE 2. Final =i= before a following =i= of an enclitic word
  is elided in =nist= (= =ni-ist=), =sei= (= =si-ei=), =niba= (=
  =ni-iba=).

  NOTE 3. Every =i= before =h= and =r= is broken to =aí=; cp. § 20.

  NOTE 4. =ij= is found in =ija=, '_eam_'; =þrija=, '_tria_';
  =fijan=, _to hate_; =frijôn=, _to luv_; =sijum=, _we ar_; =kijans=,
  _germinated_, etc. =i= for =ij= is rare: =fian=, =sium=, etc., but
  =friaþwa= (beside =frijaþwa=), _luv_, occurs very often.

  NOTE 5. Occasionally =e= takes the place of =i=; as, =usdrebi=; Mk.
  V, 10; =seneigana=; I. Tim. V, 1.

  NOTE 6. For =i= in the difthong =iu=, s. §§ 18. 19.

  NOTE 7. For a separation of the two =i=s (= OHG. ë and i) in East
  Gothic names, s. Wrede, 'Ostg.', 162.


o

§ 11. The Gothic character =o= always denotes a long close =o=
approaching sumwhat the sound of =û= (= o in E. home).

  NOTE 1. In Greek words =o=, as a rule, corresponds to ω, rarely to
  ο; e. g., =Makidonja=, Μακεδονία; it also stands for ου: =Iodas=,
  Ἰούδας; Lu. III, 26.

  NOTE 2. =o= in Gothic words often stands for (short) =u= (§ 14, n.
  3).

§ 12. =ô= (= OHG. uo; s. ahd. gr., § 38 et seq.) is frequent in Gothic
words. E. g., =brôþar=, _brother_; =bôka=, _beech_; =frôþs=, _wise_;
=flôdus=, _flud_; =fôtus=, _foot_.

In the prt. of the VI. series (§ 35) and of the =ê--ô=-series (§ 36):
=ôl=, =hôf=, =ôg=, pl. =ôlum=, =hôfum=, =ôgum=;

> From Grad Morav, in the year of Our Lord 847.

### 3.1 Noun Morphology

## 1. Historical Moment: The Glagolitic Incursion

### Context
- Mid-9th century: **Nicene (Byzantine) missionaries** arrive from Thessaloniki, bearing *Glagolitic script* and a new literary prestige tied to **Old Church Slavonic** (OCS).  
- They represent both a theological threat (Nicene orthodoxy vs. local Arian/Ulfilan Christianity) and a *cultural centralization*—imported liturgy, imported alphabet, imported saints.  
- In response, the Gothicized Moravian elites (scribes, abbots, and local princes) experience a **defensive identity crisis**:  
  “We already have letters. We already have scripture. We are not barbarians to be taught reading.”

### Consequence
→ A **revival and formalization of the local koine**, branded as the *lingua gothica slavonica* (or simply *slovo gothik*), consciously positioned as the “Western rite tongue.”

---

## 2. The Reaction: “Gothic Reform” (c. 860-890 CE)

### Goals
1. **Reassert legitimacy** through continuity with Wulfila and Latin Christendom.  
2. **Block linguistic Hellenization** by standardizing the Gothic–Slavic vernacular as *orthodox-in-form, not Nicene-in-doctrine*.  
3. **Differentiate** the local script and vocabulary from Glagolitic–OCS usage.

### Methods
- Codify orthography in a “Reformed Gothic” hand (derived from Wulfila script but adapted to Slavic phonology).  
- Purge overtly Greek calques from the lexicon.  
- Create **Gothic-based equivalents** for Nicene/Greek theological terms.  
- Reintroduce **old Gothic morphology** (-s nominative, -ōs plural, strong adjectives) as prestige markers in chancery and scripture.  
- Establish *duplex registers*:  
  - **“Gothic High”** (for law, faith, charters),  
  - **“Slovian Plain”** (for speech and local correspondence).

---

## 3. Linguistic Strategy: Calquing and Parallelism

| *zakonъ* (law) | law, canon | *reiksdom* “king-doom” | *law* vs. *statute* |
| *blagodatь* (grace) | divine favor | *gudh-mild* “God-mildness” | *grace* vs. *favor* |

---

## 1.  The *Age of the Mixed Tongues* (roughly 1120–1250)

By now, scribes and poets have generations of bilingual schooling behind them.  
The old Gothic–Slavic calquing habit turns into deliberate **word-craft**: every educated writer is part philologist, part alchemist.

Three huge forces drive the change:

1. **Printlike manuscript culture** — cheap vellum and disciplined lay copyists outside monasteries.  
2. **Secular patronage** — urban guilds, princely courts, and the itinerant theater.  
3. **A pan-lexical appetite** — access to Gothic, Latin, Greek, Slavic, Turkic, and even Avaric lexica through trade and translation.

---

## 2.  The New Arts

### The Early Novel
- Written in *slovo-narodni styl* (“speech-of-the-people style”), a blend of courtly Gothic diction and market-speech Slavic.  
- Common themes: travel between realms (*Podzemgrad* “the Under-City”), identity and disguise, love across tribes.  
- Narrators adopt **alternating voices**: one chapter in High Gothic register, one in plain folk Slovo.  
- First-person confession emerges centuries before Western Europe’s *Roman de la Rose*.

### Poetry
- The hybrid prosody allows both **alliteration** (from Gothic tradition) and **syllabic rhyme** (from Slavic verse).  
- Poets exploit etymological play:  
  *mirfriþ / bogljub / svetliuhs* alternate with new borrowings like *eros-milosť*, *psyche-duch*, *logos-slovo*.

### Theater
- Begun in cathedral courtyards as didactic pageants (*misterii mir-friþa*), but rapidly turns satirical and secular.  
- Actors speak in dialectal blends; scripts switch registers for comic or moral effect.  
- Stage directions written half in Latin, half in vernacular: *entra homo cum maska dupli-licis.*

---

## 3.  The Vocabulary Explosion

### Borrowing & Co-integration

| Source | Function | Example formation | Meaning |
|---------|-----------|------------------|----------|
| **Gothic** | heroic, archaic tone | *reik-romania* | the kingdom of stories |
| **Latin** | scholastic, scientific | *ratio-pravda* | reasoned truth |
| **Greek** | philosophical, aesthetic | *kosmo-mir*, *theo-bogos*, *trago-igra* | world, divinity, tragic play |
| **Old Church Slavonic** | liturgical flavor | *blago-friþ*, *sveto-dom* | blessed peace, holy hall |
| **Czehkish / Old Moravian** | colloquial warmth | *milu-pesň*, *domči-saga* | love-song, household tale |
| **Sorbian** | regional color | *luba-grajda* | joyful gathering |
| **Avar / Turkic** | exotic imagery, warfare | *tuman-šar*, *jan-bogat* | mist-banner, brave hero |

### Word-formation habits
- *Intercalation*: a Greek stem flanked by Gothic and Slavic affixes (*bog-theos-stvo*).  
- *Triples*: three roots from three languages fused (*dom-polis-gard* = “metropolis”).  
- *Play with sound*: Turkish loan *tuman* “fog” used for emotional haze; Slavic poets rhyme it with *human* (from Latin *humanus*).

---

## 4.  Intellectual Context

- **Universities of Nitra and Velehrad** teach the *artes duae linguae*, the twin-tongue arts: rhetoric through bilingual composition.  
- Grammarians compile comparative lexica centuries before Renaissance humanists.  
- Translation of Aristotle and Galen uses native compounds (*razum-krug*, “circle of reason”), blending Greek logic with local idiom.

---

## 5.  Cultural Climate

| Sphere | Characteristic innovation | Notes |
|--------|---------------------------|-------|
| **Music** | mixed tonal system (Slavic modes + Gothic chant) | yields early polyphony |
| **Visual arts** | inscriptions in blended scripts | pictorial calligraphy as theology |
| **Civic life** | theater guilds & readers’ lodges | literacy becomes social currency |
| **Women writers** | convent schools teaching dual grammar | earliest lyric voices in the region |

---

## 6.  The Language Itself

By the mid-thirteenth century:

- **Case endings** further level to analytic prepositions; yet writers preserve them in verse for cadence.  
- **Compound density** rivals classical Sanskrit.  
- **Loan integration** so deep that etymology becomes stylistic choice, not necessity.  
- **Phonology** stabilizes: long vowels from Gothic, palatal consonants from Slavic, front rounded vowels from Sorbian and German influence.

Scholars call this phase *Vysoka Slavogothika* — “High Slavogothic.”

## 3.  Morphological Play

Old High German and Bulgar inputs push morphology in new directions:

- **Germanic compounding precision** → long civic and legal compounds:  
  *mark-gelt-recht* “currency law,” *hand-werk-dom* “guild jurisdiction.”
- **Bulgar/Turkic agglutinative echo** → new **chain suffixes** that convey rank or relation:  
  *tarqan-nik*, *beg-stvo*, *orda-gradje*.
- **Loan phonemes**:  
  - /ts/ and /pf/ from OHG appear in technical terms;  
  - velar harmony from Turkic lends musical rhythm to epic verse.

---

## 4.  Literary Consequences

### a.  The Urban Novel
Writers in Nitra and Prague experiment with **multi-register narration**: one voice Gothic-Slavic high style, another full of OHG merchant slang or Bulgar soldier talk.  
Readers love the realism; critics call it *slovorealismus*.

### b.  Theater of Masks
Playwrights use foreign suffixes to mark character speech: a Turkic ending for mercenaries, Greek for scholars, German for tradesmen.  
The audience instantly hears social identity in morphology alone.

### c.  Philosophical Prose
At Velehrad, translators of Aristotle coin hybrids like  
*energi-dъlo* “act-work,” *forma-obraz*, *matiere-telo* — a technical vocabulary that Western Europe will not achieve until scholastic Latin two centuries later.

---

## 5.  The Sound of the Mature Tongue

Phonetically it’s a living mosaic:

- Slavic softness (palatal n, l)  
- Gothic long vowels (ō, ē)  
- OHG affricates (ts, pf)  
- Bulgar / Turkic /q, ɣ/ in loanwords  
- Rhythmic stress alternating like old verse meters

Example line from an early thirteenth-century epic:

> *Kral rechtzakon siedel v ordadomi i slušal pesen duchgeistovu o mirfriþe bogtheoswaldsa.*

**Translation:**  
> The king of lawful order sat in the camp-fort and listened to the spirit-song of the divine governance.

Every content word is multinational, yet it reads as one continuous idiom.

---

## 6.  The Cultural Picture

- **Guild literature:** manuals of architecture and trade written in mixed technical jargon — the earliest European “professional prose.”  
- **Frontier songs:** Bulgar and Turkic meters married to Slavic rhyme.  
- **Court chronicles:** OHG clerks bring documentary precision; local poets supply emotional depth.  
- **Philosophical schools:** “Reik-Theos Academy” in Nitra teaches trilingual logic centuries before the Sorbonne.

By the mid-1200s, *High Slavogothic* is a **self-conscious cosmopolitan language**, a true written koine of Central Europe.  Where Latin and Greek divide West and East, Slavogothic unites them — a tongue with *Gothic bones, Slavic flesh, German muscle, and steppe blood.*

> „Ty pisala to ne rukoj, no duchem, i ten duch jest zrodon iz vsech jazykov.  V tvoej pesni govori mir-čelovek, i jaz uslyšal ego.“  
>  
> Na tom slove morje uтихло, i tuman-oblaka raskryli dvo-sunc.  Svitliuhs pal na Lubu i Ardar, i kazdogo videnie bylo drugomu zerkalo.  
>  
> I tak načalo se povest o Lube i Ardarovi, o slovowaurde i meče, o tom kako bogtheoswalds sam naklonil neba, da by ljubostь stala zakonom, i zakon — ljubostъ.

### **English Rendering**

Beneath the shining sky of Karanpolis sailed the ship of the world-city, called *Two Suns*, and upon its deck stood the maiden Luba of Zalfmark, her eyes dark as dusk and her laughter bright as the world-light above the water.

With her was Captain Ardar Reikson, son of an old line of peace-judges, whose hand knew both sword and pen, and in whose heart burned desire not for gold, but for the word-waurd and for merciful justice.

For two days they journeyed across the sea, seeing the cloud-horde rise in the east, where the beg-tarqan had set his sacred watchtowers against King Bog-Theos-Walds.  And at evening, when the mist-banner fell upon the deck, Luba stood by the railing, holding a small manuscript in which she had written a song of love, of passion, and of gentle law-freedom.

Ardar approached softly and said with a smile:  
“Maiden Luba, your words burn like fire in snow.  Who taught you to weave runes and letters into a single cloth of love?”

She laughed and said, “No one, my captain.  I listened to the sea, and it spoke to me.  Every wave speaks in two tongues—one Slavic, one Gothic—and I interpreted them with my heart.”

Then Ardar took the book and read:

> “When two suns rise above one earth,  
> then peace-friþ shall grow in lovers’ hands.  
> God-lovehood is holier than all gods and breaks the chains of mortal hordes.”

The words were like honey and iron, like a voice-spirit and a sword of truth.  
The captain bowed his head and said,  
“You wrote this not with the hand but with the spirit, and that spirit is born of all tongues.  In your song speaks the man of peace, and I have heard him.”

At that word the sea grew still, and the mist-clouds opened the two suns.  
The world-light fell upon Luba and Ardar, and each saw in the other a mirror.  
And thus began the tale of Luba and Ardar—of word-waurd and sword, of how King Bog-Theos-Walds himself bent the heavens so that love became law, and law became love.

The ornate *High Slavogothic* prose moves like verse: parallel syntax, paired compounds, echoes of Gothic alliteration and Slavic cadence.  Its heroes speak in twin metaphors—every moral idea doubled across two etymologies.  This is the voice of the mature cosmopolitan age: half legend, half philosophy, already anticipating the psychological and rhetorical richness that later Europe would find only in Shakespeare and Goethe.
